claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Poburko et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Super-resolution microscopy has shown nanoscale protein partition of UCP4 and F1Fo-ATP synthase, residing in the inner boundary membrane and the cristae membrane, respectively, in mitochondria from neurons.
claims.source: Consistent with this model, super-resolution microscopy has shown, in the mitochondria from neurons, nanoscale protein partition of UCP4 and F1Fo-ATP synthase, residing in the inner boundary membrane and the cristae membrane, respectively (Klotzsch et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Klotzsch et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Several groups have independently proposed that F1Fo-ATP synthase is of the same molecular identity as that of mPTP.
claims.source: Several groups have independently proposed that F1Fo-ATP synthase is of the same molecular identity as that of mPTP (Giorgio et al., 2013; Alavian et al., 2014; Bonora et al., 2013; Bernardi et al., 2015), whose flickering openings signify the ignition of mitoflashes (Wang et al., 2008; Hou et al., 2014).

claims.claim: Flickering openings of mPTP signify the ignition of mitoflashes.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: UCP2 is the dominant isoform of UCPs in heart.
claims.source: Inhibition of UCP2, the dominant isoform of UCPs in heart (Ricquier and Bouillaud, 2000) (Figure 5—figure supplement 4)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ricquier and Bouillaud, 2000 and experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: A Bcl-xL-regulated proton leakage through F1Fo-ATPase has been demonstrated in hippocampal neuronal mitochondria.
claims.source: Recently, a Bcl-xL-regulated proton leakage through F1Fo-ATPase has been demonstrated with multiple approaches, including patch-clamping of sub-mitochondrial vesicles, proton flux measurement, and immunochemical demonstration of a Bcl-xL interaction with the β-subunit of ATP synthase in hippocampal neuronal mitochondria (Alavian et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2011b).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Alavian et al., 2011 and Chen et al., 2011b.

claims.claim: Mitoflash activity is a biomarker for mitochondrial energy metabolism under certain conditions.
claims.source: The generation of mitoflashes in intact cells requires the integrity of the electron transfer chain (ETC) (Wang et al., 2008); and mitoflash frequency is highly regulated over a wide dynamic range by factors including metabolic state, thus the mitoflash activity is considered a biomarker for mitochondrial energy metabolism under certain conditions (Wei et al., 2011; Pouvreau, 2010; Fang et al., 2011; Gong et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Individual mitoflashes occur only intermittently and are confined to single mitochondria.
claims.source: Individual mitoflashes occur only intermittently, and are confined to single mitochondria.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on observations described in the discussion section.

claims.claim: Mitoflashes operate in the frequency-modulatory mode, with relatively constant average amplitude and duration in different conditions.

claims.claim: A cardiac myocyte typically contains 5,000–8,000 mitochondria.

claims.source: In a cardiac myocyte typically containing 5,000–8,000 mitochondria, only a tiny portion of mitochondria undergo the flashing activity at any moment
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observed mitoflash frequency and the total number of mitochondria.

claims.claim: ATP diffuses freely in the cytosol.
claims.source: Keeping in mind that ATP diffuses freely in the cytosol, such local, stochastic ATP-negating events afford a novel mechanism to finely regulate ATP homeostasis at the cellular level.
claims.evidence: This claim is stated as established knowledge.

claims.claim: Pyruvate treatment did not induce any changes in cytosolic Ca2+.
claims.source: The lack of significant effect of Ru360 on mitoflashes in cardiomyocytes is expected because pyruvate treatment did not induce any changes in cytosolic Ca2+ and thus mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Pyruvate stimulation caused a slight decrease of mitochondrial ROS.
claims.source: Further, electrical pacing did not alter (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C) and pyruvate stimulation caused a slight decrease of mitochondrial ROS (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), indicating that ROS are unlikely a major player, either.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Electrical pacing did not alter mitochondrial ROS.
claims.source: Further, electrical pacing did not alter (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C) and pyruvate stimulation caused a slight decrease of mitochondrial ROS (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), indicating that ROS are unlikely a major player, either.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: TMRM measurement revealed little effects of pyruvate stimulation, electrical pacing, ISO treatment, and EGTA treatment on ΔΨm.
claims.source: TMRM measurement revealed little effects of these manipulations on ΔΨm, excluding changes in ΔΨm as a possible cause of the mitoflash response (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Inhibiting MCU with Ru360 did not show any significant effect on mitoflash frequency.
claims.source: Moreover, inhibiting MCU with Ru360 did not show any significant effect on mitoflash frequency (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Mitoflash is sensitive to MCU inhibition in situations when it is induced by elevations of mitochondrial Ca2+.
claims.source: However, mitoflash is sensitive to MCU inhibition in situations when it is induced by elevations of mitochondrial Ca2+, e.g., in HeLa cells under hyperosmotic stress or high cytosolic Ca2+ stimulation (in permeabilized cells) (Hou et al., 2013; Jian et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Mitoflashes can serve as a biomarker of mitochondrial respiration when substrate supply is changed and ATP demand is held constant.

results.result: Mitoflashes negatively regulate ATP production in isolated cardiac mitochondria. Inhibiting mitoflash activity with SS31, mitoTEMPO, or cyclosporin A decreased mitoflash frequency by 31-47% and enhanced ATP production by 22-25%.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C17-C24 provide converging evidence from isolated mitochondria experiments showing that pharmacological inhibition of mitoflashes consistently increases ATP production. The data show quantitative, dose-dependent effects with appropriate controls and statistical significance (Figure 1). The inverse relationship between mitoflash frequency and ATP production is well-documented.

results.result: Mitoflash activity increases in response to excess substrate supply and counteracts ATP oversupply. Pyruvate stimulation increased mitoflash frequency 12-fold compared to glucose, coinciding with transient ATP elevation followed by return to baseline despite increased oxygen consumption and NADH/FADH2 levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C25-C33 demonstrate that mitoflashes respond to metabolic substrate changes with robust, reversible increases in frequency. The temporal correlation between mitoflash activation and ATP normalization (C30-C31), combined with evidence of decreased metabolic efficiency (C32-C33), supports the regulatory role. Data from both isolated cells and perfused hearts strengthen the conclusion (Figures 2A-F).

results.result: Mitoflash activity decreases in response to increased energy demand. Electrical pacing reduced mitoflash frequency by 45-80% in a frequency-dependent manner, while β-adrenergic stimulation reduced it by 70%. ATP levels remained constant despite these manipulations.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C35-C43 provide comprehensive evidence that mitoflashes respond inversely to workload changes. The dose-response relationship with pacing frequency (C36-C38), consistency across different ATP demand manipulations (C41-C42), and maintenance of ATP homeostasis (C40, C43) all support the regulatory model. The synchronized imaging approach addresses potential motion artifacts (Figure 3).

results.result: Manipulating mitoflash activity shifts the ATP set-point. Inhibiting mitoflashes with antioxidants or SOD2 overexpression decreased mitoflash frequency by ~40% and elevated ATP levels by ~60%, with a strong inverse correlation (r = -0.96, p=0.009).
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C44-C46 demonstrate that independent manipulation of mitoflash activity (without altering substrate or workload) can shift ATP levels. Multiple interventions (SS31, mitoTEMPO, SOD2 overexpression) produce consistent directional changes. The strong statistical correlation (C46) and replication across methods strengthen causality, though the correlation is based on only 4 data points which limits robustness (Figure 4).

results.result: Bcl-xL-regulated proton leakage through F1Fo-ATP synthase mediates mitoflash regulation of ATP homeostasis. Proton leakage varied with ATP supply-demand balance (28% increase with pyruvate, 11% decrease with ISO). Bcl-xL overexpression decreased mitoflashes and increased ATP by 19%, while Bcl-xL inhibition had opposite effects. UCP2 manipulation did not affect mitoflashes.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C47-C55 provide mechanistic evidence linking Bcl-xL-sensitive proton leakage to mitoflash activity and ATP regulation. The bidirectional effects of Bcl-xL manipulation (C51-C55), exclusion of UCP2 (C50), and correlation of proton leakage with metabolic state (C47-C49) support the proposed mechanism. However, the proton leakage measurements show relatively modest changes (11-28%) and the mechanistic link between proton leakage and mitoflash triggering remains indirect (Figure 5).

results.result: Mitoflashes constitute a digital, frequency-modulated auto-regulator for ATP homeostasis. Individual mitoflashes are intermittent, confined to single mitochondria, and operate in frequency-modulatory mode with constant amplitude and duration. Only a small fraction of the 5,000-8,000 mitochondria per cardiomyocyte flash at any moment.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C65-C69 synthesize the experimental findings into a coherent model of digital ATP regulation. The characterization of mitoflash properties (C65-C66) is supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1. The distributed nature of the system (C67-C68) is consistent with observed frequencies and known mitochondrial numbers. The integration of local events affecting global ATP (C69) is logically sound given ATP diffusion properties.

results.result: Bioenergetics-dependent mechanisms dominate mitoflash regulation in cardiomyocytes over Ca2+-dependent mechanisms. Pyruvate stimulation did not alter cytosolic Ca2+ or mitochondrial ROS, electrical pacing did not change ROS or ΔΨm, and MCU inhibition had no effect on mitoflashes under these conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C75, C77 systematically exclude alternative mechanisms (Ca2+, ROS, ΔΨm) through negative control experiments. The lack of Ca2+ changes with pyruvate (C70), absence of ROS changes with pacing (C72), and ineffectiveness of MCU inhibition (C74) support the bioenergetics-dependent model. The caveat that MCU can affect mitoflashes under different conditions (C75) appropriately qualifies the conclusion (Figure 5—figure supplements 1-2).

results.result: Cardiac ATP levels remain constant despite large fluctuations in workload. The ATP content and ATP/ADP ratio were held constant regardless of pacing frequency, confirming the tightness of ATP set-point regulation in mammalian myocardium.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C8, C40 establish the fundamental phenomenon being investigated. C1 and C8 cite established literature on ATP homeostasis, while C40 provides direct experimental confirmation in the current study. The constancy of ATP across different pacing frequencies (Figure 3D) validates the experimental system and provides the context for investigating regulatory mechanisms.

results.result: Previously proposed regulators of ATP homeostasis (ADP, Pi, Ca2+) face challenges. ADP and Pi are relatively constant, MCU activity is extremely low in cardiac myocytes, MCU knockout mice show MCU is dispensable except under extreme stress, and dominant negative MCU increases rather than decreases oxygen consumption.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C11 accurately summarize prior literature on limitations of existing models for ATP regulation. These are appropriately cited background claims that establish the knowledge gap motivating the current study. The citations appear accurate based on the referenced work.

results.result: Mitoflashes are ubiquitous mitochondrial events with defined characteristics. They have been detected across eukaryotic species, consist of multiple signal components (superoxide, alkalization, redox shift, NADH/FADH2 depletion, depolarization), require intact electron transfer chain, are regulated by metabolic state, and can serve as biomarkers of mitochondrial metabolism. Protons act as mitoflash triggers.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C16, C64 provide essential background on mitoflashes from prior work by the authors and others. These are well-cited claims establishing the foundation for the current investigation. The characterization of mitoflashes is consistent with the literature and provides necessary context for interpreting the ATP regulation findings.

results.result: A single heartbeat consumes approximately 2% of cellular ATP in cardiac myocytes.
results.evaluation: Claim C34 is a cited background fact (Jacobus, 1985) used to contextualize the energy demands of pacing experiments. This is an established value in the field and appropriately supports the rationale for using pacing to manipulate ATP demand.

results.result: Proton dynamics and protein localization support the local control model of mitoflash triggering. Free protons are short-lived (~1.4 ns lifetime) and diffuse only ~2.1 nm, are extremely scarce in alkaline mitochondrial matrix (~0.4 protons per mitochondrion at pH 8.0), matrix pH buffering capacity is ~5 mM per pH unit, and super-resolution microscopy shows nanoscale separation of UCP4 and F1Fo-ATP synthase.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C59 provide biophysical context from prior work supporting the proposed mechanism. The proton dynamics (C56-C58) are appropriately cited and establish why proton source proximity matters. The super-resolution microscopy data (C59) from neurons supports spatial organization, though extrapolation to cardiac mitochondria requires caution.

results.result: F1Fo-ATP synthase may be the molecular identity of mPTP, whose flickering openings trigger mitoflashes. UCP2 is the dominant UCP isoform in heart. Bcl-xL-regulated proton leakage through F1Fo-ATPase has been demonstrated in hippocampal neuronal mitochondria.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C63 cite relevant prior work establishing molecular components of the proposed mechanism. The mPTP-ATP synthase identity (C60-C61) is appropriately qualified as a proposal from multiple groups. UCP2 dominance (C62) is confirmed by the authors' own data. The Bcl-xL mechanism (C63) from neuronal mitochondria provides precedent, though tissue-specific differences should be considered.

results.result: Mitoflashes can serve as a biomarker of mitochondrial respiration specifically when substrate supply is changed while ATP demand is held constant.
results.evaluation: Claim C76 appropriately qualifies the conditions under which mitoflashes reflect respiration versus ATP regulation. This reconciles the current findings with prior interpretations and clarifies that mitoflash function depends on experimental context. The logic is sound based on the presented data.

results.result: Mitoflashes involve multifaceted energy-consuming processes including electron diversion to superoxide production, ΔΨm dissipation, and membrane permeability loss from mPTP opening, indicating a state of futile respiration.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C79 describe the bioenergetic consequences of mitoflashes based on prior characterization. These are appropriately cited and provide mechanistic basis for how mitoflashes could negatively regulate ATP production. The inference of futile respiration (C79) logically follows from the described processes.

results.result: Potential mechanisms for mitoflash-mediated ATP regulation include reverse operation of Complex V as an ATPase during ΔμH dissipation, and activation of unknown downstream pathways that prolong OXPHOS inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C81 are explicitly speculative proposals for additional mechanisms beyond those directly tested. While plausible, these hypotheses lack experimental support in the current study. They appropriately identify areas for future investigation but should not be considered established findings.

results.result: ATP is the most important energy currency and mitochondria supply ATP at a rate of approximately 6 kg/day in the human heart.
results.evaluation: Claim C7 is a cited background fact (Neubauer, 2007) establishing the importance of ATP homeostasis. This is an established value in the field and appropriately motivates the study.
